warmup.q: Your service sends POST /authorize to a card issuer with a 2-second timeout, and the timeout fires. What do you now know about the payment?
options: The issuer never received it, so showing the customer an error is safe
The issuer is down, so the payment failed
Nothing about whether the card was charged: it may have been, may be later, or may never be
The issuer declined it and the decline was lost
warmup.why: A timeout tells you how long you waited and nothing else. The request may be lost or stuck in a queue, the issuer may have crashed or be paused, or the card was charged and the reply was lost or is still coming. In some of those worlds the card is already charged, and in some it will be charged after you gave up. An error screen invites the customer to pay again. The safe move is to keep the payment pending and resolve it with the same idempotency key.

sections.h: One computer fails whole; many computers fail in part
sections.html:
On one machine, failure is mostly all or nothing. A memory error that ECC can't correct makes the kernel panic. A null dereference in native code kills the process. A disk that can't read a block makes the system call return EIO. Hardware and operating systems are built to stop rather than carry on with a wrong answer, so a program either gets its result or finds out it didn't. When your Kotlin code calls a local function, the function returns, or throws, or the whole process is gone and nobody is left to be confused.

Put the same work on two machines and that guarantee goes away. A payment service sends an authorization to a card issuer's API across a network. Now three parts fail on their own: your process, the network between, and the issuer's process. Any one can break while the other two keep running. That is partial failure, and every lesson in this track is about living with it.

The trouble is what your process can know. It knows only the messages that have reached it. Send POST /authorize for 12.50 and wait. Either a reply arrives or nothing does. If nothing does, the request is in one of three places, each in one of two states:

  • on the way there: lost, or stuck in a queue and still coming;
  • at the issuer: crashed before it charged the card, or paused (a long garbage collection, a frozen VM) and about to charge it;
  • on the way back: the card was charged and the reply was lost, or the reply is just slow.

From your side all six look identical: a socket with no bytes in it. Waiting longer doesn't settle it. A queued request can arrive after you gave up, and a paused issuer can wake and charge the card a minute later. In the stepper below, the shop's view never changes; only the issuer's side does.

So a remote call has three outcomes, not two: yes, no and unknown. Code that turns unknown into no, for example a timeout shown to the customer as a failed payment, asks the customer to try again, and in the worlds where the card was charged that charges it twice. The rest of this lesson measures how often each world turns up and what makes an unknown safe to retry. Lesson 2 asks how long to wait before you call it unknown, and lesson 5 deals with a silent node that is still acting.

frames.say: The way out. The shop treats the timeout as unknown and retries with the same idempotency key. In the worlds where the card was charged, the issuer finds the key and returns the stored code without charging again. Where it wasn't, the retry charges it once. Either way the shop ends with one charge and an answer.

try.title: Six worlds, one view
steps: Before you run it, write down for each of the six worlds whether the card ends up charged, and whether a reply ever reaches the shop.
Run the demo from the labs folder. It plays one payment through each world with a 2-second timeout and no retry, in virtual time.
Run it again with -Pargs='3' (three attempts, same key). Which worlds now end approved, and which stay unknown? Why does the paused issuer charge only once?

code.title: from the labs folder
code.html: ./gradlew -q :sim:demo -Pmain=sfz.dist.l01.demo.SilenceDemoKt ./gradlew -q :sim:demo -Pmain=sfz.dist.l01.demo.SilenceDemoKt -Pargs='3'

try.expect:
One payment, pay-1, timeout 2,000 ms, 1 attempt(s) with the same key

world                              the client decides         the issuer charged     reply after the decision
the request is lost                unknown at 2000 ms         never                  no
the request waits 5 s in a queue   unknown at 2000 ms         once at 5050 ms        yes (1)
the issuer has crashed             unknown at 2000 ms         never                  no
the issuer is paused for 5 s       unknown at 2000 ms         once at 5050 ms        yes (1)
the reply is lost                  unknown at 2000 ms         once at 51 ms          no
the reply waits 5 s in a queue     unknown at 2000 ms         once at 51 ms          yes (1)

The second column is identical in every row; the third has three different answers. With three attempts (6 s of waiting) the two queued worlds and the paused issuer end approved at 5051 ms, while the lost request, the crash and the lost reply are still unknown at 6000 ms. The paused issuer received all three attempts at 5,000 ms and charged once, because the lab's issuer checks the key: the first copy starts the charge and the other two find it in progress.

refs.title: Designing Data-Intensive Applications, 2nd edition, chapter 9 (faults and partial failures)

video.title: Partial failure: six ways to hear nothing

sections.h: Network faults are routine, and many are partial
sections.html:
At any real scale these worlds turn up every day. The best public evidence is a survey by Peter Bailis and Kyle Kingsbury, The Network Is Reliable (2014), which collected field studies and post-mortems. In Microsoft's datacenters, a 2011 study counted about 5.2 device failures and 40.8 link failures a day, with a median of about 59,000 packets lost per failure. Redundant links and switches helped less than you'd hope: during failures they raised the median traffic delivered by only 43%. Google's Chubby lock service had 61 outages in 700 days, and 4 of the 9 that lasted longer than 30 seconds came from network maintenance.

Many faults are partial. One Broadcom network card dropped every inbound packet while it kept sending. Its node kept sending heartbeats, so its standby never took over, and the service was down for five hours. In November 2020 a switch at Cloudflare failed halfway: its control-plane protocols stayed up while it forwarded only some traffic. The etcd cluster behind Cloudflare's control plane couldn't keep a stable leader and went read-only, and the knock-on effects degraded its API and dashboard for 6 hours 33 minutes. Cloudflare's post-mortem called it a Byzantine failure; it was an omission fault, messages that didn't arrive, which ordinary consensus protocols are designed to survive (lesson 7 sorts out the kinds of fault).

What do partitions do to software that passed its tests? Alquraan and colleagues (OSDI 2018) studied 136 failures caused by network partitions in 25 widely used systems, among them MongoDB, Elasticsearch, Redis, Kafka, ZooKeeper, RabbitMQ, HDFS and Cassandra. 80% were catastrophic, with data loss the most common result (26.6%). 90% were silent: the client got no error at all. 21% left damage that stayed after the network healed. Leader election was the mechanism at fault in 39.7%.

Two of their numbers should change how you test. 88% of the failures needed only one node to be isolated, and 62% happened every time, so a cheap, targeted test would have found them. And 28.7% needed a partial partition: A can reach B, and B can reach C, but A can't reach C. A test that splits a cluster cleanly in two never produces that.

A word on names. A network partition means some nodes can't reach some others for a while. It has nothing to do with partitioning data across shards (the Partitioning track). Partitions also come one way at a time: a link that carries requests and loses replies, like that network card. The Try cuts one direction only and counts what the client believes against what the issuer did.

try.title: Cut one direction
steps: 1,000 payments, one every 10 ms. Predict: if 30% of the replies are lost and the requests all arrive, how many of the unknown payments were charged? And if 30% of the requests are lost instead?
Run the demo with oneway. The audit compares the client's outcomes with the issuer's own list of charges.
Look at the unknown column in the first two rows, then at unknown, charged. Rerun with -Pargs='oneway 0.05' to see the same split at a loss rate closer to a bad day in production.

sections.html:
The Computer networking track showed how TCP turns lost, duplicated and reordered packets into a clean byte stream (its lessons on UDP and on TCP performance). Every byte has a sequence number, the receiver acknowledges what arrived, the sender resends what wasn't acknowledged after a retransmission timeout, and the receiver drops duplicate segments and puts the rest in order. So why doesn't TCP make the six worlds go away?

Because TCP's promises live inside the two kernels and end with one connection. Three gaps matter.

First, a TCP ACK means the bytes reached the issuer's kernel and sit in its socket receive buffer. It says nothing about the issuer's application. The process can crash a microsecond later with your request unread, or charge the card and crash before it writes the reply. Only an answer from the application, charged, code A00042, tells you the work happened.

Second, TCP can't tell you what happened when it gives up. If ACKs stop coming, Linux keeps retransmitting with exponential backoff, 15 times by default (net.ipv4.tcp_retries2), which takes at least 924.6 seconds, before it reports an error. Your HTTP client's timeout fires long before that. Either way you learn that the connection is dead, not which of your bytes the application acted on.

Third, TCP's duplicate detection works only within one connection. When your client times out and retries, it opens a new connection or takes another one from the pool and sends the request again. To TCP that's a new byte stream with new sequence numbers. To the issuer it's a second request. A load balancer that retries for you does the same, and so does a queue that redelivers a message.

So the application needs the same three pieces TCP has, one level up: a unique id for each operation (an idempotency key), an answer that only the application sends, and a receiver that remembers the ids it has handled. The issuer stores the key with the charge; a retry with the same key gets the stored answer back and no second charge. The networking track's production lesson introduced idempotency keys for safe retries. Here you can count what they save: in the Try, retries cut the unknowns from 344 to 45 and charged 175 cards twice, and the same retries with the key checked charged none twice.

Two details make the key work. Create it once per payment, before the first attempt, and reuse it in every retry: a new key per attempt is no key. And the server must record the key in the same transaction as the effect. If it charges the card, crashes, and never wrote the key, the next retry charges again. The Derived data track's lesson on the end-to-end argument follows this from the client all the way to storage.

try.title: Retries with and without the key
steps: 20% of packets are lost in each direction. Predict how many cards get charged twice when the client tries up to 3 times and the issuer doesn't check the key.
Run the demo with retries. Rows 2 and 3 are the same run except for the key check; rows 4 and 5 lose nothing but duplicate 20% of packets, as a retrying proxy would.
Find the cost of retries in the unknown, charged column of row 2: why can those 37 payments still not be resolved by the client?

sections.h: Delay has no ceiling, because packet networks queue
sections.html:
If every packet arrived within d milliseconds and the issuer always answered within r, a timeout of 2d + r would be exact: silence after that would mean failure, never slowness. Real networks give you no d. A packet that usually takes half a millisecond inside a datacenter can take seconds.

Follow one packet and count the queues it can wait in:

  • A switch port. When several senders send to one destination at once, the switch pushes one packet at a time onto that port and queues the rest; when the queue is full it drops the next one (the figure). A query that fans out to 100 servers and gets 100 answers back at the same instant does exactly this.
  • The receiving kernel. If every core is busy or the application's threads are all taken, arriving data waits in the socket's receive buffer, and new connections wait in the accept queue (the networking track's TCP connections lesson).
  • The hypervisor. In a VM, your virtual CPU can be taken away while another tenant's VM runs, and packets for you wait until you get a core back. On a busy host that can be tens of milliseconds.
  • TCP itself. Congestion control holds data back at the sender when it thinks the path is full, and a lost segment is resent only after a retransmission timeout, at least 200 ms on Linux. TCP turns loss into delay.

Every one of these queues grows fastest when its resource is nearly full, which is when you are busiest. At the extreme, a switch failure at GitHub in 2012 blocked traffic for 90 seconds.

Why build networks like this? The phone network didn't. A call reserved a fixed slice of every link on its path for the whole call, a circuit, so nothing queued and the delay was fixed. The price is that the slice sits idle whenever nobody talks. Data traffic is bursty: a page load, then nothing, then a 50 MB file. Packet switching lets every sender share every link and absorbs bursts in queues, so links run close to full, and the price is delay that varies without a fixed limit. Bounded delay can be bought (InfiniBand's link-level flow control, priority classes, admission control), but public clouds and the internet don't sell it to you.

So no timeout separates slow from dead. In the Try, 2% of packets in each direction wait up to 3 seconds and nothing is lost. A 100 ms timeout leaves 35 of 1,000 payments unknown, all of them charged; a 5-second timeout leaves none unknown, and makes the shop wait 5 seconds on every call to an issuer that really is dead. Lesson 2 picks the number from measurements and lets it adapt.

Run the demo. It first measures 10,000 round trips with no timeout at all, then runs 1,000 payments with timeouts from 100 ms to 5 s.
Rerun with -Pargs='0.05 10000' (5% of packets, up to 10 s). Is there still a timeout that is both safe and short?

10,000 payments, nothing lost, 2% of packets queued for up to 3000 ms
round trip including 50 ms of work: p50 56 ms, p90 59 ms, p99 2329 ms, p99.9 2944 ms, max 3053 ms

timeout     approved   unknown   unknown, charged  late replies
100 ms           965        35                 35            35
200 ms           966        34                 34            34
500 ms           973        27                 27            27
1000 ms          977        23                 23            23

The median round trip is 56 ms and the p90 is 59, but the p99 is 2.3 seconds: about 4% of round trips hit a queue in one direction or the other. Every unknown payment was charged, and every one of them got a late reply, because nothing was lost. Only a timeout longer than the longest queue (the model caps it at 3 s) leaves nothing unknown. With -Pargs='0.05 10000' the p99 is 9.2 s, the max 17.8 s (two long waits in a row), and even a 5-second timeout leaves 57 of 1,000 payments unknown: on a real network, with no cap at all, there is no timeout that is both short and safe.

refs.title: Bailis and Kingsbury: The Network Is Reliable (the GitHub and Microsoft cases)

analogy: You post an order and a cheque to a supplier and hear nothing for two weeks. The letter may be lost, or sitting in a sorting office, or on the desk of a clerk who is on holiday; or the goods shipped and the confirmation went astray. Post a second order and you may get two crates. So you write an order number on every letter and ask the supplier to ignore any number it has already filled, and a repeat letter costs nothing. The analogy breaks on scale: the post loses one of your letters a year, while a payment service sends thousands of requests a second through queues that change every microsecond, so the rare worlds happen every few minutes, and nobody reads each case by hand.
world: Every remote call your services make has the third outcome. When a Quarkus REST client call to the issuer times out, leave the payment pending, not failed, and let a background job settle it by retrying with the same idempotency key or asking the issuer for that key's status. Temporal retries an activity until it succeeds unless you limit it (its default retry policy has no maximum number of attempts), so an activity that calls an issuer must send a key that stays the same across attempts: the workflow id plus the activity's purpose, or the run id and activity id Temporal gives you. A Kafka producer that retries after a timeout can write a record twice unless idempotence is on, which the Messaging track's second producer lesson covers. And when a JDBC commit to Oracle fails with a connection error, you don't know whether it committed. Oracle's Transaction Guard records a logical transaction id for exactly this case, so after a recoverable error you can ask the database for that transaction's outcome instead of guessing.
mistake: The common mistake is treating a timeout as a failure. The code catches SocketTimeoutException or HttpTimeoutException, marks the payment FAILED and shows the customer an error. The customer pays again, and if the first request was charged and only its reply was lost, the card is now charged twice. People write it this way because local calls train us to think in two outcomes, and because tests rarely lose a reply. The fix: give every remote call three outcomes (approved, declined, unknown), keep the payment pending on unknown, and resolve it with a retry or status query that reuses the payment's idempotency key, which the issuer stores in the same transaction as the charge. Never create a new key for a retry.

compare.title: Two outcomes against three

a.label: Timeout means failed
a.title: PaymentService.kt
a.html: fun pay(order: Order): Status = try { val code = issuer.authorize(order.amount) // a new request every time Status.Approved(code) } catch (e: HttpTimeoutException) { Status.Failed // the customer is told to try again }

b.label: Timeout means unknown
b.title: PaymentService.kt
b.html: fun pay(order: Order): Status { val key = order.paymentKey // made once, when the order was created repeat(3) { try { return Status.Approved(issuer.authorize(key, order.amount)) } catch (e: HttpTimeoutException) { // unknown: the same key makes the next attempt safe } } return Status.Pending // a job resolves it later with the same key }

compare.note: The left version is shorter and wrong in two worlds out of six: when the reply was lost or slow, the card was charged and the customer is told it wasn't. The right version never reports failure on a timeout. It retries with the key the order already carries, and if every attempt times out it parks the payment as pending for a job that retries or asks the issuer for the key's status. It is only correct if the issuer stores the key with the charge; a key the server ignores turns these retries into double charges.

worked.title: A client and an issuer that survive the six worlds

steps.say: Simplest version: send and wait for the reply. On a lost request this waits until TCP gives up, which on Linux is more than 15 minutes, holding a thread and a pooled connection the whole time.
steps.code: val reply = http.send(request, BodyHandlers.ofString()) // no timeout: can block for 15+ minutes

steps.say: Bound the wait. Now the call returns, but the catch block has to decide what a timeout means, and it doesn't mean declined.
steps.code: val request = HttpRequest.newBuilder(issuerUri) .timeout(Duration.ofSeconds(2)) // until the response headers arrive .POST(BodyPublishers.ofString(body)) .build()

steps.say: Make the key part of the payment, not of the attempt. It is created when the order is, stored with it, and sent as a header on every attempt.
steps.code: val key = order.paymentKey // e.g. a UUID saved with the order val request = HttpRequest.newBuilder(issuerUri) .header("Idempotency-Key", key) .timeout(Duration.ofSeconds(2)) .POST(BodyPublishers.ofString(body)) .build()

steps.say: On the issuer, insert the key and the charge in one transaction. A unique constraint on the key turns a second copy into a conflict instead of a second charge.
steps.code: INSERT INTO charges (idempotency_key, card, amount, code) VALUES (:key, :card, 1250, :code) ON CONFLICT (idempotency_key) DO NOTHING; -- 0 rows: this key was charged already -- then, in the same transaction: SELECT code FROM charges WHERE idempotency_key = :key;

steps.say: Return what's stored, not what was just computed. The first attempt and every retry get the same code, so the client can't tell (and doesn't need to know) which attempt did the work.
steps.code: fun authorize(key: String, card: String, amount: Long): String = tx { insertIfAbsent(key, card, amount, newCode()) // the step above codeFor(key) // the one stored code for this key }

lab.title: A network that loses, delays and duplicates, and the client that copes
steps: Read Network.kt (given): send draws loss, delay, queueing and duplication for each packet from one seeded Random, so a seed replays a run exactly. Nothing sleeps; a simulated minute takes milliseconds. Then run the tests from the labs folder: all 13 fail.
Exercise 3 first, because it is the referee: write audit in Payments.kt. It compares the client's outcomes with the issuer's charges. The 2 tests in AuditTest pass.

Exercise 1: write PaymentServer.onRequest. Without dedupe, charge every copy; with it, return the stored code for a known key, ignore a key whose charge is in progress, and store the code under the key before replying. No new test passes yet: every scenario needs a client.

Exercise 2: write PaymentClient.authorize and onReply. Send attempt 1, schedule a timeout with sim.after(timeoutMs), and when it fires either retry with the same key or record Outcome.Unknown. A reply for a key already decided counts as late. Run all 13, including the jqwik properties, which try hundreds of seeds and fault rates.

Read the test a dead issuer and a paused issuer look the same to the client: two worlds, identical outcomes, opposite truths. Then change dedupe = true to false in an idempotency key makes the same retries safe and watch it fail with the double charges you counted in the Try.
hints: audit: charges.groupingBy { it.key }.eachCount() gives charges per key. Extra charges are count - 1 summed over keys.
Keep one Pending(amount, attempts) per key. In the timeout callback, if (key in outcomes) return@after handles the reply that came in time.
Don't put the retry logic in onReply. Only the timeout decides to retry; a reply only decides Approved or counts a late reply.
In onRequest, add the key to working before calling charge, and move it to codes inside the charge callback. A copy that arrives while the charge runs must not start a second one.

drill.title: The idempotent issuer from memory
drill.prompt: Close the lab. Write the issuer's onRequest with deduplication: a known key gets its stored code, a key in progress gets nothing, a new key is charged once. Then add one comment: what goes wrong if the real issuer writes the key to its database in a separate transaction after the charge?

answer.html: private val codes = mutableMapOf<String, String>() // key -> code, once charged private val working = mutableSetOf<String>() // keys being charged now fun onRequest(from: String, request: AuthRequest) { val known = codes[request.key] when { known != null -> reply(from, request.key, known) // a retry or a copy: same answer request.key in working -> Unit // the first copy's reply is coming else -> { working += request.key charge(request) { code -> codes[request.key] = code // remember, then answer working -= request.key reply(from, request.key, code) } } } } // A separate transaction leaves a gap: charge committed, crash, key never written. // The next retry finds no key and charges the card again. Key and charge commit together.

recap: A distributed system fails in part: your process, the network and the remote process each break on their own, and your process knows only the messages it received.
Silence after a request has six causes (lost, queued, crashed, paused, reply lost, reply slow) that look identical. A remote call has three outcomes: yes, no and unknown.

Network faults are routine and often partial or one-way. Alquraan et al. found 80% of partition failures catastrophic, 90% silent, 88% triggered by isolating one node and 28.7% needing a partial partition.
TCP's guarantees end at the kernel and at one connection: an ACK isn't an application answer, and a retry over a new connection is a new request.
Packet networks queue in switches, kernels, hypervisors and TCP itself, so delay has no upper bound and no timeout separates slow from dead.
Retries are safe only with an idempotency key made once per operation and stored in the same transaction as its effect.

explain.prompt: A teammate says: "We use TCP, so requests can't be lost or duplicated. We don't need idempotency keys." Explain what TCP does guarantee, where that guarantee ends, and what happens to a payment when it ends.
explain.answer: TCP guarantees that within one connection the bytes arrive in order, once, or that the connection fails. It does that inside the two kernels with sequence numbers, ACKs and retransmission. The guarantee ends in two places. First, at the application: an ACK means the issuer's kernel has our bytes, not that the issuer charged the card. It can crash after reading the request, or after charging and before replying. Second, at the connection: when our client times out, it retries over a new connection, and TCP has no idea it's the same request, so the issuer sees two. Between those two gaps there are worlds where the card was charged and we never heard, and a retry then charges it again. So we need the same trick TCP uses, one level up: a key per payment that every attempt carries, stored by the issuer in the same transaction as the charge, so a repeat returns the first result. And when we still have no answer, the payment is pending, not failed.

deeper.html:
Testing for partial partitions. Alquraan and colleagues built NEAT, a partition-injection framework, and used it to find and report 32 new failures in 7 systems, including Ceph, ActiveMQ and Infinispan. Their follow-up (Alfatafta et al., OSDI 2020) focused on partial partitions alone and proposed Nifty, a layer that reroutes traffic through nodes that can still reach both sides, to make any system tolerate them. The cheapest version for your own services is a test that blocks one direction between two specific containers, with iptables or Toxiproxy, while a third container can still reach both.

Bounded delay, where you can buy it. InfiniBand uses credit-based flow control on every link, so a switch never sends a packet the next hop has no room for, and nothing is dropped for lack of buffer. Datacenter Ethernet can do something similar per priority class (priority flow control). On the internet, the L4S architecture (RFCs 9330 to 9332) marks packets before queues fill so that senders slow down early, which keeps queueing delay low without reserving capacity. None of these gives a hard upper bound across a public cloud, which is why the next lesson measures rather than assumes.

The book's framing. Designing Data-Intensive Applications, 2nd edition, chapter 9, makes the same argument about unreliable networks and the limits of TCP, with more field data. This lesson's numbers come from the primary sources it cites and from the lab.
